definition:
The intermediate state is the condition of a person between death and the resurrection of the body at Christ's return. The phrase is a theologians' term, not a biblical one, and it names a real question: if the Christian hope is the resurrection of the body at the end, what happens to those who die before then? The New Testament's answer, as most of the church has read it, is that believers who die are with Christ, consciously and blessedly, in a state Paul calls “far better” (Philippians 1:23), and yet that state is not the end. It is a waiting, the person still without the body God means to raise. The Old Testament knows far less, speaking mainly of Sheol, the realm of the dead, with a slowly growing trust that God's hold on his people does not end at the grave. Christians have differed about the nature of the waiting: whether the dead are conscious, whether there is purification after death, and how prayer for the dead fits. They agree that the resurrection, not the intermediate state, is the final hope.

The Hebrew vocabulary begins with she'ol, used about sixty-five times, the place or condition of the dead, pictured as below the earth, dark, and silent. Its origin is uncertain, and it is not a place of punishment as such; righteous Jacob expects to go there (Genesis 37:35). Parallel terms include bor, 'pit', and qever, 'grave', and the rephaim, the 'shades' or 'departed spirits' of the dead (Isaiah 14:9; Psalm 88:10). The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, usually rendered she'ol as hadēs, the name for the underworld in Greek religion, and hadēs appears ten times in the Greek New Testament. The New Testament adds paradeisos, 'Paradise', a Persian loanword for a walled park or garden, used in the Septuagint for the garden of Eden and three times in the New Testament (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 12:4; Revelation 2:7). It also speaks of the dead as 'fallen asleep' (koimaomai), a common Jewish and Greek way of speaking of death, which in Christian use carries the added sense that the sleeper will wake.
ot:
Israel's first word about death is sober. The man made from dust returns to dust (Genesis 3:19), and the patriarchs die and are “gathered to his people” (Genesis 25:8), a phrase used of Abraham before his burial and distinct from it, which suggests joining the ancestors rather than simply entering the tomb. The common destination is Sheol. Jacob, mourning Joseph, says “I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son” (Genesis 37:35). Several psalms speak of Sheol as a place where praise is silent: “For there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?” (Psalm 6:5), and Psalm 88 asks, “Can Your loving devotion be proclaimed in the grave, Your faithfulness in Abaddon?” (Psalm 88:11). Hezekiah prays in the same terms (Isaiah 38:18). Ecclesiastes is starker still: “the dead know nothing” (Ecclesiastes 9:5), and in Sheol “there is no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom” (Ecclesiastes 9:10). These texts describe death from the side of the living, and many interpreters read them as laments rather than doctrine about the dead's inner state: what is lost at death is life before God in the land of the living, the worship, work, and relationships that make up a life. They are not a full theology of the afterlife, and they do not claim to be. Ecclesiastes itself ends with a different note: “the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

Some passages give the dead a shadowy existence. Isaiah's taunt against the king of Babylon imagines Sheol stirring “the spirits of the dead to greet you” (Isaiah 14:9), the former kings rising from their thrones to mock the fallen tyrant. The law forbids anyone to consult “a medium or spiritist, or inquires of the dead” (Deuteronomy 18:11), a prohibition that assumes such practices were known and treats them as rebellion against God, the only rightful source of guidance. The one narrative in which the dead appear is the story of Saul and the medium of Endor (1 Samuel 28), in which Samuel comes up and announces Saul's death. Readers since the early church have differed over it: some hold that God truly permitted Samuel to appear, others that a deceiving spirit took his likeness, and others that the medium staged what she claimed; all agree that the story condemns Saul's act.

Alongside the silence runs a conviction that God is not absent from death. “If I make my bed in Sheol, You are there” (Psalm 139:8). The LORD “brings down to Sheol and raises up” (1 Samuel 2:6). Enoch was taken by God (Genesis 5:24), and Elijah went up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). A few psalms reach toward a communion with God that death does not break. “God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself” (Psalm 49:15). “You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory” (Psalm 73:24), and “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26). Isaiah says that the righteous who die “find rest, lying down in death” (Isaiah 57:2). Scholars debate how much of an afterlife these texts affirm, but they show that for Israel's faith the relationship with God was the heart of the matter, and it was hard to believe that God would let it end.

By the time of Jesus, Jewish writers had developed these hints in several directions. In 1 Enoch 22, a text from the third or second century BC, the dead are kept in separate hollow places until the judgment, the righteous apart from the wicked. The Wisdom of Solomon, a book in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament, says that the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God and at peace (Wisdom 3:1-3). In 2 Maccabees 12:43-45 Judas Maccabeus has an offering made for fallen soldiers, in the hope of the resurrection, a text later important to the Catholic teaching on prayer for the dead. Josephus reports that the Pharisees taught that souls survive death and receive reward or punishment, while the Sadducees held that the soul perishes with the body (Jewish War 2.163-165; Antiquities 18.14-16).
nt:
Jesus spoke of the dead as alive to God. Answering the Sadducees, he said that God's word to Moses at the bush, 'I am the God of Abraham', shows that “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Mark 12:27), and Luke adds, “for to Him all are alive” (Luke 20:38). His main point is the resurrection, but the argument assumes that the patriarchs are not simply gone. At the transfiguration “Moses and Elijah appeared before them, talking with Jesus” (Matthew 17:3). He warned his disciples not to fear “those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28), which assumes that a person is not wholly destroyed when the body dies. In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, the poor man dies “and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side” (Luke 16:22), while the rich man is in Hades, in torment, and “a great chasm has been fixed” between them (Luke 16:26). It is a parable, and interpreters caution against drawing a map of the afterlife from its scenery, which uses images common in Jewish teaching of the time; but Jesus chose a story in which the dead are conscious, their states are fixed, and the living still have Moses and the Prophets. Most directly, to the dying criminal who asked to be remembered, Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43). He himself died praying, “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit” (Luke 23:46), and Stephen died praying, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59).

Jesus also entered death. Peter preached that Psalm 16 was fulfilled in him: “You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (Acts 2:27). Paul speaks of Christ descending “to the lower parts of the earth” (Ephesians 4:9), and 1 Peter says that Christ, “put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit”, went and “preached to the spirits in prison” (1 Peter 3:18-19). That passage is among the most debated in the New Testament. Augustine read it as Christ preaching by his Spirit through Noah to the people of Noah's day; many early and later readers took it as Christ proclaiming his victory to the dead between his death and resurrection; and William Dalton's study (1965) argued that it describes the risen Christ announcing his triumph over the rebellious spirits of Genesis 6. The risen Christ holds “the keys of Death and of Hades” (Revelation 1:18).

Paul gives the fullest account of the believer's death. He often calls it sleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14; 1 Corinthians 15:18, 20), as Jesus did of Lazarus (John 11:11-14), a figure that speaks of death's peace and temporariness and of the certainty of waking. Yet he also says that death brings a believer into Christ's presence. “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21), and he desires “to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed” (Philippians 1:23). In 2 Corinthians 5 he contrasts the present body, an “earthly tent”, with “a building from God, an eternal house in heaven” (2 Corinthians 5:1), and says that he does not wish “to be unclothed but clothed” (2 Corinthians 5:4). Most interpreters take the 'unclothed' state as the soul without the body between death and resurrection, which Paul does not desire for its own sake, though he still says he would “prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8). Others read the heavenly house as the resurrection body received at death. On either reading, being with the Lord is the heart of it. Paul's words about being caught up to Paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2-4) confirm that Paradise was for him a real place of God's presence.

The later books confirm the pattern. Hebrews speaks of the believer's worship as joining “the spirits of the righteous made perfect” (Hebrews 12:23) and says “man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). In Revelation, John sees “the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God” (Revelation 6:9) under the heavenly altar. They are conscious, they cry out “How long, O Lord” for justice, and they are given white robes and told “to rest a little while longer” (Revelation 6:10-11). The dead in the Lord are blessed, for “they will rest from their labors” (Revelation 14:13). Then, at the end, “Death and Hades gave up their dead” (Revelation 20:13) and are thrown into the lake of fire. The intermediate state is real, it is good for those in Christ, and it is temporary. It ends at the resurrection.

keyTexts.why: Abraham dies, is gathered to his people, and is buried. The Old Testament speaks of death as joining the ancestors, a phrase distinct from burial itself.
Saul consults a medium and Samuel appears to pronounce judgment. The story assumes the dead exist and condemns seeking them out.
Death shepherds the proud to Sheol, but the psalmist trusts that God will redeem his life from Sheol and take him to himself.
The psalmist trusts that God will receive him in glory and remain his portion forever when flesh and heart fail. Communion with God reaches past death.
The dead know nothing and in Sheol there is no work or knowledge. The Teacher speaks from the side of the living and presses the reader to live fully now.
The shades in Sheol rise to greet the fallen king of Babylon. The poetic taunt shows how Israel pictured the realm of the dead.
Jesus argues from God's covenant name that God is the God of the living. The patriarchs, though dead, are still bound to him.
In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus the dead are conscious, their states differ, and a chasm divides them. Interpreters debate how much of its imagery to press.
Jesus promises the dying criminal Paradise today and dies committing his spirit to his Father. It is the church's main text for immediate presence with Christ.
Stephen, dying, sees the glory of God and asks Jesus to receive his spirit, and then falls asleep. The two ways of speaking of death stand side by side.
Paul longs to be clothed with the heavenly dwelling rather than left unclothed, and prefers to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
Paul weighs life and death and calls departing to be with Christ far better. The text most clearly implies conscious fellowship with Christ at death.
Paul calls the Christian dead those who sleep and promises that God will bring them with Jesus. The sleep is real rest and certain waking.
The worshiping church draws near to the heavenly Jerusalem and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect. The dead in Christ belong to the one assembly.
The souls of the martyrs under the altar cry out for justice, receive white robes, and are told to rest a little longer. They are with God and still waiting.

history:
The early church held that the dead await the resurrection, but it spoke of their waiting in more than one way. Justin Martyr, in his Dialogue with Trypho (about 160, chapter 80), counted as no true Christians those who deny the resurrection and say that souls are taken up to heaven at death, which shows how firmly resurrection was held to be the final hope. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.31) taught that the souls of the faithful go to an invisible place appointed by God and wait there for the resurrection, as Christ himself went to the place of the dead for three days. Tertullian (On the Soul, chapter 55, early third century) held that only the martyrs go straight to Paradise, while others wait in the underworld. Christians prayed for their dead from early times, as tomb inscriptions and the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (about 203), in which Perpetua sees her dead brother relieved after her prayers, both show. Augustine (Enchiridion 109-110, about 421) taught that between death and resurrection souls are kept in hidden places of rest or affliction, and that the prayers and Eucharists of the church help some of the departed. The Apostles' Creed's clause that Christ 'descended to the dead' is first attested around 400, in the creed of Aquileia described by Rufinus.

The Western church developed the teaching on purgatory. Gregory the Great (Dialogues book 4, about 593) taught a purifying fire after death for lesser sins. The historian Jacques Le Goff argued (The Birth of Purgatory, 1981) that purgatory as a distinct place, with the noun purgatorium, took shape in the late twelfth century, though Catholic scholars stress the continuity of the underlying belief with earlier prayer for the dead. A profession of faith received at the Second Council of Lyon (1274), and then the Council of Florence (1439), taught that those who die in grace but not yet fully purified are cleansed after death and helped by the prayers of the living; at Florence the Greek bishop Mark of Ephesus resisted the Latin teaching of a purgatorial fire. In 1331 and 1332 Pope John XXII preached that the blessed dead would not see God fully until the last judgment, which provoked strong opposition, and his successor Benedict XII defined in Benedictus Deus (1336) that the souls of the saints who need no purification see God's essence immediately after death. The Fifth Lateran Council (1513) condemned the teaching that the individual soul is mortal.

The Reformation began in a dispute about indulgences, which were tied to purgatory, when Luther published his Ninety-five Theses in 1517. The Reformers came to reject purgatory as having no basis in Scripture and as undermining the sufficiency of Christ's work: Luther in the Smalcald Articles (1537), the Church of England in Article 22 of the Thirty-Nine Articles (1563), and the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 32), which teaches that the souls of the righteous are received at once into the highest heavens and those of the wicked into hell, and that Scripture acknowledges no other place. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, Question 57) confesses that the believer's soul is taken immediately to Christ its head. The Council of Trent's decree on purgatory (1563) reaffirmed it while ordering bishops to suppress superstition and financial abuse around it. Among the Reformers, Luther often spoke of death as a deep sleep; William Tyndale argued against Thomas More (1531) that placing the departed already in heaven weakens the argument for the resurrection; John Calvin wrote Psychopannychia (completed 1534, published 1542) against Anabaptists who taught that souls sleep; and the Church of England's Forty-Two Articles (1553) condemned soul sleep in an article later dropped. Christian mortalism, the view that the whole person dies and awaits the resurrection, was held by Richard Overton (Man's Mortality, 1644) and John Milton, and later by the Seventh-day Adventist Church. In the twentieth century Oscar Cullmann (1955) described the dead in Christ as sleeping yet near to Christ, and debate over body and soul has continued between defenders of dualism such as John W. Cooper (Body, Soul, and Life Everlasting, 1989) and Christian physicalists such as Nancey Murphy (Bodies and Souls, or Spirited Bodies?, 2006) and Joel B. Green (Body, Soul, and Human Life, 2008).

differ.body: At death the believer's soul goes at once into the presence of Christ, conscious, at rest, and blessed, while the body rests in the grave until the resurrection. Defenders point to Jesus' promise of Paradise “today” (Luke 23:43), Paul's desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), his preference to be away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), the spirits of the righteous made perfect (Hebrews 12:23), and the conscious souls under the altar (Revelation 6:9-11). The state is good but incomplete, since the person still awaits the body. This is the teaching of the Heidelberg Catechism and the Westminster Confession, of Calvin, and of most Protestant churches, and in its core, the immediate blessedness of those fully purified, of Benedict XII's Benedictus Deus as well.

The Catholic Church teaches that those who die in God's grace and friendship but are not yet fully purified undergo a purification after death, so as to reach the holiness needed to enter the joy of heaven; this purification is entirely different from the punishment of the damned (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1030-1031). It rests on the church's practice of prayer for the dead from its earliest centuries, on 2 Maccabees 12:43-46, on Jesus' words about sin not forgiven 'in the age to come' (Matthew 12:32), and on Paul's image of a person saved “as if through the flames” (1 Corinthians 3:15). Defenders stress that purgatory is a work of grace, not of human merit: Christ's love finishing what it began. Benedict XVI (Spe Salvi, 2007) described it as the purifying encounter with Christ himself, and some Protestants, such as Jerry Walls (Purgatory: The Logic of Total Transformation, 2012), have argued for a form of it as sanctification completed.

The Orthodox Church holds that the departed are conscious and that they experience a foretaste of their final state, joy or sorrow, before the last judgment. It prays for the departed, especially in memorial services and on the third, ninth, and fortieth days after death, trusting that the prayers of the church help them, while declining the Western definition of purgatory as a place of satisfaction for temporal punishment. Mark of Ephesus defended this position at the Council of Florence (1439). The Orthodox appeal to the church's ancient liturgies, which commemorate the dead in every Eucharist, and to the fathers, and they leave much about the condition of the departed undefined. Some Orthodox writers have used the tradition of 'toll-houses' to picture the soul's passage after death, a teaching other Orthodox theologians reject.

Some Christians hold that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, either because the soul sleeps or because the whole person dies and is kept in God's memory until he raises them. Defenders point out that Scripture repeatedly calls death sleep (Daniel 12:2; John 11:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:13), that the Old Testament says the dead know nothing (Ecclesiastes 9:5), and that the New Testament places reward and life at the resurrection, not at death (John 6:40; 1 Corinthians 15:18). They read Luke 23:43 as 'Truly I tell you today, you will be with Me in Paradise', since the Greek manuscripts had no punctuation, and they hold that for the one who dies, the next moment of awareness is the resurrection, so Paul could speak of departing and being with Christ. Views of this kind were held by some Anabaptists, by Richard Overton and John Milton, and by the Seventh-day Adventist Church, and some Christian physicalists hold related positions.

errors:
The church has rejected the attempt to contact the dead. The law forbade mediums and spiritists (Deuteronomy 18:10-11), and Saul's visit to Endor is told as the last step of his ruin. Spiritualism and seances, which spread widely in the nineteenth century, fall under the same prohibition: the living are not to seek guidance from the dead but from God. The church has also rejected teachings that make death the end of the person, whether in the materialist form that denies any future or in forms that deny the resurrection, and it rejects reincarnation, since “man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). It rejects the popular notion that the dead become angels; angels and human beings are different creatures, and the redeemed are raised as human beings. Justin's warning still applies to any piety in which going to heaven at death replaces the resurrection as the final hope.

Within the church, Protestants and Catholics have disagreed sharply about purgatory, but both have rejected the abuses that surrounded it. The sale of spiritual benefits, and any teaching that suggests grace can be purchased or that the living can buy a soul's release, was condemned by the Reformers and by the Council of Trent itself. The church has also warned against over-precise maps of the afterlife. Dante's Divine Comedy is a great poem, not a revelation; the New Testament tells believers far less about the intermediate state than about the resurrection, and what it tells them is enough: those who die in the Lord are with the Lord.
life:
This doctrine matters most at deathbeds and gravesides. It lets Christians say two things at once without contradiction: that a believer who has died is with Christ, which is far better, and that death is still an enemy whose defeat is not yet complete. Grief is not faithlessness, because the separation is real and the body lies in the ground. Comfort is not denial, because the one who has died is not lost. The late medieval tradition of the ars moriendi, the 'art of dying', taught Christians to prepare for death by confession, prayer, and trust in Christ, and the instinct behind it remains sound: to live aware that life is short and that God holds both sides of death.

The Apostles' Creed confesses 'the communion of saints', and Hebrews speaks of a great cloud of witnesses (Hebrews 12:1). Christians who differ about prayer for the dead can agree that the dead in Christ belong to the same body as the living, that they rest from their labors, and that they are waiting for the same morning. The prayers of the living can therefore be full of thanksgiving for those who have died in faith, and of longing for the day when, as Paul says, the dead in Christ will rise and we will be with the Lord together.
questions: Many psalms describe Sheol as a place of silence where no one praises God. Why do you think the Old Testament speaks so honestly about death before the fuller hope of the New Testament?
How can Paul call death both sleep and departing to be with Christ, which is far better? What do the two images each protect?

Christians differ over purgatory, prayer for the dead, and soul sleep, but agree that the resurrection is the final hope. How should that shared hope shape the way believers grieve and remember those who have died?
